```{r fc inits, eval = T}
# Initial values for possible states
# "NA" for the latent state at all places before an individual was observed

cjs.init <- function(ch, fc){
  inits <- ch    #initialize with observations up until states diverge from observations (4yr olds)
  for(i in 1:dim(ch)[1]) {
    # for(i in 1:10) { 
    inits[i,fc[i]] <- NA #pups at release
      if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=1){   
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 1)] <- 2} #1 yr old
      if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=2){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 2)] <- 3}  #2 yr old
      if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=3){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 3)] <- 4} #3 yr old
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=4){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 4)] <- 5}
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=5){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 5)] <- 6}
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=6){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 6)] <- 7}
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=7){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 7)] <- 8}
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=8){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 8)] <- 9}
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=9){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 9)] <- 10}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=10){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 10)] <- 11}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=11){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 11)] <- 12}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=12){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 12)] <- 13}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=13){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 13)] <- 14}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=14){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 14)] <- 15}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=15){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 15)] <- 16}
    
    if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=16){
        inits[i,(fc[i] + 16)] <- 17}
    
      if(n_occasions-fc[i]>=17) {
        inits[i,((fc[i] + 17):n_occasions)] <- 18} #all 17yrs+ are plus group
  } #i
  return(inits)
}

### TMB alive/dead version
#change from age-based states to 0's and 1's
yf <- ifelse(y == 19, 0, 1)

#z.init: 0's before tagging and after last seen, otherwise 1
get_z_init <- function(y, fc) {
  
  n_ind <- nrow(y)
  # n_occ <- ncol(y)
  
  z_init <- matrix(0, nrow = n_ind, ncol = n_occ)
  
  for (i in 1:n_ind) {
    last_seen <- suppressWarnings(max(which(y[i, ] == 1)))
    
    # If seen again after tagging
    if (is.finite(last_seen) && last_seen > fc[i]) {
      z_init[i, fc[i]:last_seen] <- 1
    } else {
      # If never seen again, it is only known to be alive on the tagging day
      z_init[i, fc[i]] <- 1 
    }
  }
  return(z_init)
}

# Run on binary observation data
z.init.f <- get_z_init(yf, fc)
z.init.m <- get_z_init(ym, fc_m)

get_last_seen <- function(y, fc) {
  n_ind <- nrow(y)
  last_seen <- numeric(n_ind)
  for (i in 1:n_ind) {
    ls <- suppressWarnings(max(which(y[i, ] == 1)))
    if (is.finite(ls) && ls > fc[i]) {
      last_seen[i] <- ls
    } else {
      last_seen[i] <- fc[i]
    }
  }
  return(last_seen)
}

last_seen_f <- get_last_seen(yf, fc)
last_seen_m <- get_last_seen(ym, fc_m)
```

```{r stable age average, eval = T}

# calculate the average pup count of the first 8 years to capture the fact that age structure 
# might not be stable
avg_early_pups <- mean(pup_cnt_filled$US_PupCnt[1:8])

phi_P <- 0.68
phi_1 <- 0.8
phi_J <- 0.85 # juveniles (Ages 2-5)
phi_A <- 0.92 # adults (Ages 6-13)
phi_AA <- 0.78
phi_AM <- 0.8
phi_AAM <- 0.4

# storage
N_f_track <- matrix(0, nrow = 25, ncol = (n_occasions-1))
N_m_track <- matrix(0, nrow = 20, ncol = (n_occasions-1))

# Use actual year 1 count for pups, build the adults from the average
N_f_track[1, 1] <- round(pup_cnt_filled$US_PupCnt[1] / 2)
N_m_track[1, 1] <- pup_cnt_filled$US_PupCnt[1] - N_f_track[1, 1]

# Create a dummy average pup base for calculating adults
base_f_pups <- round(avg_early_pups / 2)
base_m_pups <- avg_early_pups - base_f_pups

# build the adults using the smoothed base
for (a in 1:24) {
  surv <- ifelse(a == 1, phi_P, 
          ifelse(a == 2, phi_1, 
          ifelse(a >= 3 & a <= 5, phi_J,
          ifelse(a >= 6 & a <= 12, phi_A, phi_AA))))
          
  if(a == 1) {
    N_f_track[a + 1, 1] <- round(base_f_pups * surv)
  } else {
    N_f_track[a + 1, 1] <- round(N_f_track[a, 1] * surv)
  }
}

for (a in 1:19) {
  surv <- ifelse(a == 1, phi_P, 
          ifelse(a == 2, phi_1, 
          ifelse(a >= 3 & a <= 5, phi_J,
          ifelse(a >= 6 & a <= 12, phi_AM, phi_AAM))))
          
  if(a == 1) {
    N_m_track[a + 1, 1] <- round(base_m_pups * surv)
  } else {
    N_m_track[a + 1, 1] <- round(N_m_track[a, 1] * surv)
  }
}

N_f_init <- N_f_track
N_m_init <- N_m_track

N_f_init[1, ] <- NA
N_m_init[1, ] <- NA

init_pop_f <- N_f_track[, 1]
init_pop_m <- N_m_track[, 1]
```

```{r IPM fec_t sst, eval = T, results = 'hide', message = F, warning = F}

csl_ipm <- function(par) {
  
  ### DATA
  
  yf <- dat$yf                 
  ym <- dat$ym
  fc <- dat$fc               
  fc_m <- dat$fc_m 
  last_seen_f <- dat$last_seen_f
  last_seen_m <- dat$last_seen_m
  
  y_pup_counts <- dat$pup_counts 
  sst_pup <- dat$sst_pup
  sst_np <- dat$sst_np
  
  n_fem <- nrow(yf)
  n_m <- nrow(ym)
  n_occ <- ncol(yf)
  max_age_f <- 24
  max_age_m <- 19
  
  nll <- 0 
  
  
  ### PARAMETERS & PRIORS
  
  b_DD <- exp(par$log_b_DD)
  
  # nll <- nll + b_DD # the negative log-likelihood of an Exponential(1) is +x
  nll <- nll - dnorm(par$log_b_DD, mean = log(0.1), sd = 0.25, log = TRUE) #could do 0.01
  
  ## bounding SDs to prevent precision matrix explosion in Laplace
  sd_cnt  <- exp(par$log_sd_cnt) + 10       #estimated variance; floor at 10
  # sd_cnt <- dat$sd_cnt #stronger trust in counts as a census 
  
  #add prior to penalize large sd's
  nll <- nll - dnorm(par$log_sd_cnt, mean = 8, sd = 1.5, log = TRUE)
  
  sigma_fec <- exp(par$log_sigma_fec) + 0.01 # Floor at 0.01 for the random effect
  eps_fec <- par$eps_fec
  nll <- nll - sum(dnorm(eps_fec, mean = 0, sd = sigma_fec, log = TRUE))
  
  ##ridge penalties
  pup_mus <- c(par$muP, par$muPM)
  
  all_mus <- c(par$mu1, par$mu2_3, par$mu4_6, par$mu7_9, par$mu10_12, 
               par$mu_fec,
               # par$muP, par$muPM,
               par$b_warm,
               par$mu13_16, par$muA, par$mu1M, par$mu2_3M, par$mu4_6M, 
               par$mu7_9M, par$mu10_12M, par$mu13_16M, par$muAM, par$mup1, 
               par$mup2_3, par$mup4_6, par$mup7_12, par$mupA, par$mup1M, 
               par$mup2_3M, par$mup4_6M, par$mup7_12M, par$mupAM)
               
  # Group all environmental covariate slopes
  all_bssts <- c(par$b_sstP, par$b_sst1, par$b_sst2_3, par$b_sst4_6, par$b_sst7_9, 
                 par$b_sst10_12, par$b_sst13_16, par$b_sstA, par$b_sst2_3M, 
                 par$b_sst4_6M, par$b_sst7_9M, par$b_sst10_12M, par$b_sst13_16M, 
                 par$b_sstAM)
                 
  # nll <- nll - sum(dnorm(pup_mus, mean = qlogis(0.70), sd = 0.5, log = TRUE))
   nll <- nll - sum(dnorm(pup_mus, mean = 0, sd = 1, log = TRUE))
  
  # Apply N(0, sd = 1.5) prior to all logits, probabilities heavily bound between 0.05 and 0.95 
  nll <- nll - sum(dnorm(all_mus, mean = 0, sd = 1.5, log = TRUE))
  
  # Shrink slopes toward 0 to prevent covariate overfitting
  nll <- nll - sum(dnorm(all_bssts, mean = 0, sd = 1.0, log = TRUE))
  
  
  # POPULATION PROJECTION
  
  N_f <- vector("list", n_occ)
  N_m <- vector("list", n_occ)
  expected_pups <- numeric(n_occ)
  phif_pop <- vector("list", n_occ)
  phim_pop <- vector("list", n_occ)
  pf_pop   <- vector("list", n_occ)
  pm_pop   <- vector("list", n_occ)
  real_phiP <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phiPM <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi1 <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi1M <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi2_3 <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi2_3M <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi4_6 <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi4_6M <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi7_9 <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi7_9M <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi10_12 <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi10_12M <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi13_16 <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phi13_16M <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phiA <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  real_phiAM <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  lreal_fec <- numeric(n_occ-1)
  Ntot <- numeric(n_occ)
  
  N_f[[1]] <- dat$init_pop_f 
  N_m[[1]] <- dat$init_pop_m
  Ntot[1] <- sum(N_f[[1]])+sum(N_m[[1]])
  
  lp1    <- par$mup1
  lp2_3  <- par$mup2_3
  lp4_6  <- par$mup4_6
  lp7_12 <- par$mup7_12
  lpA    <- par$mupA
  lp1M    <- par$mup1M
  lp2_3M  <- par$mup2_3M
  lp4_6M  <- par$mup4_6M
  lp7_12M <- par$mup7_12M
  lpAM    <- par$mupAM
  
  p1    <- plogis(par$mup1)
  p2_3  <- plogis(par$mup2_3)
  p4_6  <- plogis(par$mup4_6)
  p7_12 <- plogis(par$mup7_12)
  pA    <- plogis(par$mupA)
  pf_vec <- c(0, p1, rep(p2_3, 2), rep(p4_6, 3), rep(p7_12, 6), rep(pA, 12))
  
  p1M    <- plogis(par$mup1M)
  p2_3M  <- plogis(par$mup2_3M)
  p4_6M  <- plogis(par$mup4_6M)
  p7_12M <- plogis(par$mup7_12M)
  pAM    <- plogis(par$mupAM)
  pm_vec <- c(0, p1M, rep(p2_3M, 2), rep(p4_6M, 3), rep(p7_12M, 6), rep(pAM, 7))
  
  for (t in 1:n_occ) {
    pf_pop[[t]] <- pf_vec
    pm_pop[[t]] <- pm_vec
  }
  
  for (t in 1:(n_occ - 1)) {
    N_curr_f <- N_f[[t]]
    N_curr_m <- N_m[[t]]
    
    N_scaled <- (sum(N_curr_f) + sum(N_curr_m)) / 100000 
    
    # in case of NAs, not necessary
    curr_sst_pup <- ifelse(is.na(sst_pup[t]), 0, sst_pup[t])
    curr_sst_np  <- ifelse(is.na(sst_np[t]), 0, sst_np[t])
    
    phiP <- plogis(par$muP + par$b_sstP * curr_sst_pup - b_DD * N_scaled)
    phi1 <- plogis(par$mu1 + par$b_sst1 * curr_sst_np)
    phi2_3 <- plogis(par$mu2_3 + par$b_sst2_3 * curr_sst_np)
    phi4_6 <- plogis(par$mu4_6 + par$b_sst4_6 * curr_sst_np)
    phi7_9 <- plogis(par$mu7_9 + par$b_sst7_9 * curr_sst_np)
    phi10_12 <- plogis(par$mu10_12 + par$b_sst10_12 * curr_sst_np)
    phi13_16 <- plogis(par$mu13_16 + par$b_sst13_16 * curr_sst_np)
    phiA <- plogis(par$muA + par$b_sstA * curr_sst_np)
    
    phif_vec <- c(phiP, phi1, rep(phi2_3, 2), rep(phi4_6, 3), rep(phi7_9, 3),
                  rep(phi10_12, 3), rep(phi13_16, 4), rep(phiA, 8))
    phif_pop[[t]] <- phif_vec 
    
    phiPM <- plogis(par$muPM + par$b_sstP * curr_sst_pup - b_DD * N_scaled)
    phi1M <- plogis(par$mu1M + par$b_sst1 * curr_sst_np)
    phi2_3M <- plogis(par$mu2_3M + par$b_sst2_3M * curr_sst_np)
    phi4_6M <- plogis(par$mu4_6M + par$b_sst4_6M * curr_sst_np)
    phi7_9M <- plogis(par$mu7_9M + par$b_sst7_9M * curr_sst_np)
    phi10_12M <- plogis(par$mu10_12M + par$b_sst10_12M * curr_sst_np)
    phi13_16M <- plogis(par$mu13_16M + par$b_sst13_16M * curr_sst_np)
    phiAM <- plogis(par$muAM + par$b_sstAM * curr_sst_np)
    
    phim_vec <- c(phiPM, phi1M, rep(phi2_3M, 2), rep(phi4_6M, 3), rep(phi7_9M, 3),
                  rep(phi10_12M, 3), rep(phi13_16M, 4), rep(phiAM, 3))
    phim_pop[[t]] <- phim_vec 
    
    N_next_adults_f <- N_curr_f[1:24] * phif_vec[1:24]
    N_next_adults_m <- N_curr_m[1:19] * phim_vec[1:19]

    # fec_t <- plogis(par$mu_fec + eps_fec[t])
    lfec_t <- par$mu_fec + (par$b_warm * curr_sst_np) + eps_fec[t]
    fec_t <- plogis(lfec_t)
     # fec_t <- plogis(par$mu_fec + (par$b_warm * curr_sst_np))
    lreal_fec[t] <- lfec_t
    expected_pups[t+1] <- sum(N_curr_f[6:24]) * fec_t
    
    real_phiP[t] <- phiP
    real_phiPM[t] <- phiPM
    real_phi1[t] <- phi1
    real_phi1M[t] <- phi1M
    real_phi2_3[t] <- phi2_3
    real_phi2_3M[t] <- phi2_3M
    real_phi4_6[t] <- phi4_6
    real_phi4_6M[t] <- phi4_6M
    real_phi7_9[t] <- phi7_9
    real_phi7_9M[t] <- phi7_9M
    real_phi10_12[t] <- phi10_12
    real_phi10_12M[t] <- phi10_12M
    real_phi13_16[t] <- phi13_16
    real_phi13_16M[t] <- phi13_16M
    real_phiA[t] <- phiA
    real_phiAM[t] <- phiAM
    
    # if y_pup_counts is missing or out of bounds; not necessary
    if (!is.na(y_pup_counts[t+1])) {
      new_pups <- y_pup_counts[t+1]/2
    } else {
      new_pups <- expected_pups[t+1]/2
    }
    
    N_f[[t+1]] <- c(new_pups, N_next_adults_f)
    N_m[[t+1]] <- c(new_pups, N_next_adults_m)
    Ntot[t+1] <- sum(N_f[[t+1]]) + sum(N_m[[t+1]])
  }
  
  # aerial count likelihood 
  for (t in 2:n_occ) {
    if (!is.na(y_pup_counts[t])) {
      nll <- nll - dnorm(y_pup_counts[t], expected_pups[t], sd_cnt, log = TRUE)
    }
  }
  
  # MARK RECAPTURE LIKELIHOOD 
  
  # --- FEMALES ---
  for (i in 1:n_fem) {
    if (last_seen_f[i] > fc[i]) {
      for (t in (fc[i] + 1):last_seen_f[i]) {
        age_s <- min(t - fc[i], max_age_f + 1)
        age_d <- min(t - fc[i] + 1, max_age_f + 1)
        
        phi <- phif_pop[[t - 1]][age_s]
        p   <- pf_pop[[t]][age_d]
        
        nll <- nll - log(phi + 1e-10)
        if (yf[i, t] == 1) {
          nll <- nll - log(p + 1e-10)
        } else {
          nll <- nll - log(1 - p + 1e-10)
        }
      }
    }
    
    if (last_seen_f[i] < n_occ) {
      chi <- 1 
      for (t in n_occ:(last_seen_f[i] + 1)) {
        age_s <- min(t - fc[i], max_age_f + 1)
        age_d <- min(t - fc[i] + 1, max_age_f + 1)
        
        phi <- phif_pop[[t - 1]][age_s]
        p   <- pf_pop[[t]][age_d]
        
        chi <- (1 - phi) + (phi * (1 - p) * chi)
      }
      nll <- nll - log(chi + 1e-10)
    }
  }
  
  # --- MALES ---
  for (i in 1:n_m) {
    if (last_seen_m[i] > fc_m[i]) {
      for (t in (fc_m[i] + 1):last_seen_m[i]) {
        age_s <- min(t - fc_m[i], max_age_m + 1)
        age_d <- min(t - fc_m[i] + 1, max_age_m + 1)
        
        phi <- phim_pop[[t - 1]][age_s]
        p   <- pm_pop[[t]][age_d]
        
        nll <- nll - log(phi + 1e-10)
        if (ym[i, t] == 1) {
          nll <- nll - log(p + 1e-10)
        } else {
          nll <- nll - log(1 - p + 1e-10)
        }
      }
    }
    
    if (last_seen_m[i] < n_occ) {
      chi <- 1 
      for (t in n_occ:(last_seen_m[i] + 1)) {
        age_s <- min(t - fc_m[i], max_age_m + 1)
        age_d <- min(t - fc_m[i] + 1, max_age_m + 1)
        
        phi <- phim_pop[[t - 1]][age_s]
        p   <- pm_pop[[t]][age_d]
        
        chi <- (1 - phi) + (phi * (1 - p) * chi)
      }
      nll <- nll - log(chi + 1e-10)
    }
  }
  
  # Back-transform and summarize baseline vital rates
  b_warm <- par$b_warm
  real_phiPM_med <- mean(real_phiPM)
  real_phiP_med <- mean(real_phiP)
  real_phi1M_med <- mean(real_phi1M)
  real_phi1_med <- mean(real_phi1)
  real_phi2_3M_med <- mean(real_phi2_3M)
  real_phi2_3_med <- mean(real_phi2_3)
  real_phi4_6M_med <- mean(real_phi4_6M)
  real_phi4_6_med <- mean(real_phi4_6)
  real_phi7_9M_med <- mean(real_phi7_9M)
  real_phi7_9_med <- mean(real_phi7_9)
  real_phi10_12M_med <- mean(real_phi10_12M)
  real_phi10_12_med <- mean(real_phi10_12)
  real_phi13_16M_med <- mean(real_phi13_16M)
  real_phi13_16_med <- mean(real_phi13_16)
  real_phiAM_med <- mean(real_phiAM)
  real_phiA_med <- mean(real_phiA)
  
  int.phiP   <- plogis(par$muP)
  int.phi1   <- plogis(par$mu1)
  int.phi2_3   <- plogis(par$mu2_3)
  int.phi4_6   <- plogis(par$mu4_6)
  int.phi7_9   <- plogis(par$mu7_9)
  int.phi10_12   <- plogis(par$mu10_12)
  int.phi13_16   <- plogis(par$mu13_16)
  int.phiA   <- plogis(par$muA)
  
  int.phiPM   <- plogis(par$muPM)
  int.phi1M   <- plogis(par$mu1M)
  int.phi2_3M   <- plogis(par$mu2_3M)
  int.phi4_6M   <- plogis(par$mu4_6M)
  int.phi7_9M   <- plogis(par$mu7_9M)
  int.phi10_12M   <- plogis(par$mu10_12M)
  int.phi13_16M   <- plogis(par$mu13_16M)
  int.phiAM   <- plogis(par$muAM)
  
  int.p1   <- plogis(par$mup1)
  int.p2_3   <- plogis(par$mup2_3)
  int.p4_6   <- plogis(par$mup4_6)
  int.p7_12   <- plogis(par$mup7_12)
  int.pA   <- plogis(par$mupA)
  
  int.p1M   <- plogis(par$mup1M)
  int.p2_3M   <- plogis(par$mup2_3M)
  int.p4_6M   <- plogis(par$mup4_6M)
  int.p7_12M   <- plogis(par$mup7_12M)
  int.pAM   <- plogis(par$mupAM)
  
  lfec <- mean(lreal_fec)

  #reports
  ADREPORT(sd_cnt)
  ADREPORT(Ntot)
  ADREPORT(expected_pups)
  ADREPORT(lfec)
  ADREPORT(lreal_fec)
  ADREPORT(real_phiP_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phiPM_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi1_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi1M_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi2_3_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi2_3M_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi4_6_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi4_6M_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi7_9_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi7_9M_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi10_12_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi10_12M_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi13_16_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phi13_16M_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phiA_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phiAM_med)
  ADREPORT(real_phiP)
  ADREPORT(real_phiPM)
  ADREPORT(real_phi1)
  ADREPORT(real_phi1M)
  ADREPORT(real_phi2_3)
  ADREPORT(real_phi2_3M)
  ADREPORT(real_phi4_6)
  ADREPORT(real_phi4_6M)
  ADREPORT(real_phi7_9)
  ADREPORT(real_phi7_9M)
  ADREPORT(real_phi10_12)
  ADREPORT(real_phi10_12M)
  ADREPORT(real_phi13_16)
  ADREPORT(real_phi13_16M)
  ADREPORT(real_phiA)
  ADREPORT(real_phiAM)
  ADREPORT(int.phiP)
  ADREPORT(int.phi1)
  ADREPORT(int.phi2_3)
  ADREPORT(int.phi4_6)
  ADREPORT(int.phi7_9)
  ADREPORT(int.phi10_12)
  ADREPORT(int.phi13_16)
  ADREPORT(int.phiA)
  ADREPORT(int.phiPM)
  ADREPORT(int.phi1M)
  ADREPORT(int.phi2_3M)
  ADREPORT(int.phi4_6M)
  ADREPORT(int.phi7_9M)
  ADREPORT(int.phi10_12M)
  ADREPORT(int.phi13_16M)
  ADREPORT(int.phiAM)

  ADREPORT(lp1)
  ADREPORT(lp2_3)
  ADREPORT(lp4_6)
  ADREPORT(lp7_12)
  ADREPORT(lpA)
  ADREPORT(lp1M)
  ADREPORT(lp2_3M)
  ADREPORT(lp4_6M)
  ADREPORT(lp7_12M)
  ADREPORT(lpAM)
  
  ADREPORT(b_DD)
  ADREPORT(sigma_fec)
  ADREPORT(b_warm)

  return(nll)
}
```

```{r load tmb IPM results, eval = T}
preds_all <- data.frame()
sst_pup_vals <- list(min(sst_dat[,2]), max(sst_dat[,2]))
sst_np_vals <- list(min(sst_dat[,4]), max(sst_dat[,4]))
sst_names <- c('low', 'high')

for (c in 1:length(sst_pup_vals)) { #low vs high vals of covariate

    cov_val_pup <- sst_pup_vals[[c]]
    cov_val_np <- sst_np_vals[[c]]
    
    # logit_p <- qlogis(outmat[, 'int.phiP']) + outmat[, 'b.sst.P']*cov_val_pup
    logit_p <- ests[ests$variable == 'muP', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sstP', 'Estimate']*cov_val_pup
    logit_1 <- ests[ests$variable == 'mu1', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sst1', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_2.3 <- ests[ests$variable == 'mu2_3', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sst2_3', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_4.6 <- ests[ests$variable == 'mu4_6', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sst4_6', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_7.9 <- ests[ests$variable == 'mu7_9', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sst7_9', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_10.12 <- ests[ests$variable == 'mu10_12', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sst10_12', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_13.16 <-ests[ests$variable == 'mu13_16', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sst13_16', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_A <- ests[ests$variable == 'muA', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_sstA', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    logit_f <- ests[ests$variable == 'mu_fec', 'Estimate'] + ests[ests$variable == 'b_warm', 'Estimate']*cov_val_np
    
    preds_p <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_p), rate = 'P')
    preds_1 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_1), rate = '1')
    preds_2 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_2.3), rate = '2.3')
    preds_3 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_4.6), rate = '4.6')
    preds_4 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_7.9), rate = '7.9')
    preds_5 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_10.12), rate = '10.12')
    preds_6 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_13.16), rate = '13.16')
    preds_7 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_A), rate = 'A')
    preds_8 <- data.frame(estimate = plogis(logit_f), rate = 'Fec')
    
    preds <- bind_rows(preds_p, preds_1, preds_2, preds_3, preds_4, preds_5, 
                       preds_6, preds_7, preds_8) %>%
      mutate(cov = sst_names[c])
    
    preds_all <- bind_rows(preds_all, preds)
}

preds <- preds_all %>%
  group_by(rate, cov) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(med = median(estimate),
                   lower = quantile(estimate, probs = 0.025),
                   upper = quantile(estimate, probs = 0.975)) %>%
  transform(rate = factor(rate, levels = c('P', '1', '2.3', '4.6', '7.9', '10.12', '13.16', 'A', 'Fec'), 
                          labels = c('0-1', '1-2', '2-4', '4-7', '7-10', '10-13', '13-17', '17+', 'Fec'))) %>%
  transform(cov = factor(cov, levels = c('low', 'high'), labels = c('Low', 'High')))
                   
sst_preds_hilo_plot <- ggplot(preds, aes(x = cov, y = med)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
                show.legend = F, width = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(group = rate), linewidth = 0.7, linetype = 'dashed', position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +

  labs(x = "SST",

  theme(legend.position = 'none',
                axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 7))) +
```

```{r projection and K, eval = T}
  Metric = factor(rep(c("Theoretical K", 'Realized K', "Empirical MNPL"), each = length(theoretical_K)),
                  levels = c("Theoretical K", 'Realized K', "Empirical MNPL")))

    # subtitle = "Derived from deterministic projections (SST = 0)",

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

### summary metrics

N_current_draws <- rnorm(n = n_draws, mean = (Ntot[Ntot$year == (n_occ-1), "Estimate"]),
                                              sd = (Ntot[Ntot$year == (n_occ-1), "Std_Error"]))

osp_ratios <- mean(N_current_draws/empirical_MNPL)

mean_osp_ratio <- mean(osp_ratios)
ci_osp_ratio <- quantile(osp_ratios, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

#probability stock is above OSP (ratio >= 1.0)

summary_table <- round(data.frame(

    N_LCI = Ntot[Ntot$year == (n_occ-1), "lower"],
    N_UCI = Ntot[Ntot$year == (n_occ-1), "upper"],
    MNPL = empirical_MNPL_mean,
    MNPL_UCI = empirical_MNPL_CI[1],
    MNPL_LCI = empirical_MNPL_CI[2],
```

#### Introduction 

CSL as indicator species in a dynamic CCE 
- Importance of monitoring sentinel species to understand population dynamics, provide updated management and conservation metrics, and understand responses of a species sensitive to environmental variability in an ecosystem notorious for cyclic phases  
- Climate impacts the food web and health  
- Opportunities afforded by a well-studied (and observable) species in a dynamic environment  

Estimating density dependence for long-lived top predator  
- Challenges  
- Different approaches  

CSL historical and contemporary context  
- ups and downs and connections with ENSO  
- prominent species along the coast  
- foraging ecology/fisheries interactions  
- human impacts and disease/stranding/public concern  

Current importance  
-- estimates growing outdated  
-- improvements upon previous estimation, and more SST evidence  

Aims: update/upgrade Laake et al. and provide management metrics    
- Laake et al implemented a two-step approach: survival estimates fed into population projection model and then separately derive K and MNPL.    
-- Benefits: computationally efficient.   
-- Disadvantages: (1) does not fully integrate uncertainty in MR estimates within the population projection model and therefore does not resolve discrepancies between the two datasets based on relative precision of the data streams; (2) DD not estimated with respect to a particular vital rate (doesn't specify mechanism of dependence) and assumes downturns in abundance are due to density instead of environmental effect.      
- Fully integrated IPM addresses these issues: (1) weights uncertainty in each data stream to settle discrepancies; uncertainty from all components propagated into final posteriors of *K* and MNPL, and (2) estimates DD with respect to an ecological mechanism and facilitates specifying how transient dynamics (such as small cohort of pups from ENSO event) propagates through the age structure over the subsequent decade.     
- Full IPM distinguishes between ENSO noise and density signal - what would *K* be in an average environment -- may be a higher/truer carrying capacity instead of logistic growth model where a lot of high SST years could look like approaching *K*.    
<!-- - In the IPM, MNPL and *K* are emergent properties derived from age-structured vital rates. Laake et al. used the $\theta$ parameter to mold the productivity curve into a specific mathematical shape, which could skew MNPL relative to *K* (generally 0.6 for marine mammals instead of 0.5K that would be represented by perfect symmetry) whereas the IPM will organically generate right-skewed productivity curve based on vital rates   -->
- Ultimately, this model enhances ecological realism.

##### Statistical analyses

We developed a fully integrated population model (IPM) using a frequentist, maximum marginal likelihood framework to jointly estimate vital rates and population dynamics for California sea lions using data collected from the California Coast from 1990-2025. The IPM framework simultaneously evaluates a Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS; citation) mark-recapture model and a deterministic demographic projection matrix, linked by age- and sex-specific survival parameters and annual pup counts to constrain the demographic estimates.

*Vital rates subcomponent model*

We modeled individual capture histories using a CJS framework to estimate age- and sex-specific apparent survival ($\phi$) and detection probabilities ($p$). The state process was modeled using a categorical distribution tracking individuals across distinct biological age classes, up to a maximum modeled lifespan of 24 and 19 years for females and males, respectively.

Survival probabilities were estimated for pups, ages 1, 2-3, 4-6, 7-9, 10-12, 13-16, and 17+ for both males and females. Survival probabilities were estimated on the logit scale and modeled as a function of baseline age- and sex-specific intercepts ($\mu$) and environmental stochasticity ($\beta_{\text{SST}}$). Additional temporal variation not attributable to the effects of SST were not included and pup birth weight, while known to be influential in survival outcomes, was not included as a covariate here due to its correlation with annual SST (i.e., pup weights negatively correlated with SST; citation or create additional supplemental figure). Because density dependence in pinnipeds acts most strongly on early life stages (i.e., pups), the density effect ($\beta_{\text{DD}}$) was isolated to pup survival ($\phi_P$). Total annual population size, $N_t$, was the summation of all male and female age classes and scaled by a constant ($100,000$) to facilitate convergence. For an individual $i$ at time $t$ and sex $s$, pup survival was parameterized as:

$$\text{logit}(\phi_{p, i, t}) = \mu_p + \beta_{\text{SST}_p} \cdot \text{SST}_{t} - \beta_{\text{DD}} \cdot \left( \frac{N_{t}}{100,000} \right)$$

Juvenile and adult survival and fecundity were assumed to be density-independent and driven solely by baseline rates and environmental effects. Thus, survival for older age classes (yearlings through adults) was parameterized with age-specific intercepts and distinct sea surface temperature values ($\text{SST}_{t}$) relevant to foraging ecology:

$$\text{logit}(\phi_{a, i, t}) = \mu_a + \beta_{\text{SST}, a} \cdot \text{SST}_{t}$$

Detection probabilities ($p$) were assumed to be constant between sexes for yearlings and estimated separately for each sex and age class on the logit scale. 

$$\text{logit}(\p_{a, i}) = \mu^{\text{p}}_a$$

In the mark-resight subcomponent model, we assumed that marks were not lost, misread, or missed when an animal is encountered, and that all individuals within a specific age and sex class share the same underlying probabilities of survival and detection in a given year.

*Population projection subcomponent model*

To evaluate population-level dynamics, we constructed a sex-specific stochastic projection model using survival rates estimated as above. 

The initial population size for the first year of the time series was assigned deterministically from field observations and baseline stable age distribution approximations. Population structure and age-specific abundance for each subsequent age class $a$ were modeled deterministically using the predicted annual age-specific survival probabilities (${\phi}_{a, t}$), which dynamically updated based on changes in SST and density dependence over the study period, multiplied by the age-specific abundance in the previous year:

$$N_{a+1, t+1} = {\phi}_{a, t}\cdot N_{a, t}$$

Individuals reaching the terminal age classes (age 24, age 19) were assumed to undergo complete reproductive and survival senescence and were removed from the matrix in subsequent time steps. Females could reproduce up until age 23.

*Integrated population model*  

To link the unobserved adult female population to the observed pup counts, we modeled reproduction using a post-breeding census assumption. Pups born in year $t+1$ were calculated as a function of the females that successfully survived into year $t+1$.

Fecundity was estimated as a single time-varying rate applied to reproductively active females (Ages 5–23), modified by both a linear environmental covariate ($\beta_{\text{warm}}$) and an annual random effect ($\epsilon_{\text{fec}, t}$) to absorb temporal process variance. Assuming an equal sex ratio at birth, the expected total number of pups produced was calculated as:

$$E[Pups_{t+1}] = \sum_{a=5}^{24} N_{f, a, t+1} \cdot \text{logit}^{-1}(\mu_{\text{fec}} + \beta_{\text{warm}} \cdot \text{SST}_{t} + \epsilon_{\text{fec}, t})$$

The final integration of the demography and the count data was achieved by evaluating the expected pup production in terms of the aerial census data ($y_{t+1}$) using a Gaussian likelihood with an estimated variance parameter ($\sigma_{\text{count}}$):

$$y_{t+1} \sim \text{Normal}(E[Pups_{t+1}], \sigma_{\text{count}})$$

Assuming the mark-recapture data ($\mathbf{y}_{MR}$) and the pup census counts ($\mathbf{y}_{count}$) are conditionally independent, the joint marginal likelihood of the model ($L_{IPM}$) is the product of their separate likelihoods, integrating over the unobserved random effects:

$$L_{IPM}(\theta\vert{}\mathbf{y}_{MR},\mathbf{y}_{count})= \iint L_{MR}(\theta\vert{}\mathbf{y}_{MR})\times L_{count}(\theta, \epsilon_{\text{fec}}\vert{}\mathbf{y}_{count}) d\epsilon_{\text{fec}}$$

where $\theta$ represents the joint vector of all fixed effects (survival, detection, fecundity, observation variance, and environmental/density coefficients). By evaluating this joint likelihood, the model allows the pup census data to inform and constrain the vital rates that cannot be fully resolved by the mark-recapture data alone.  

To address structural identifiability challenges inherent in complex integrated population models, we employed ridge penalties (L2 regularization) within the objective function. In models where primarily a single demographic stage is observed without error (e.g., the annual pup census), latent vital rate parameters can be confounded. Specifically, the model can achieve the exact same expected pup count by estimating extremely high baseline fecundity balanced by strong density-dependent pup mortality, or conversely, low fecundity paired with negligible density dependence. Left unconstrained, these parameter "seesaws" create flat likelihood surfaces (identifiability ridges) where the optimizer may fail to converge, wander into biologically impossible parameter space, or yield non-positive definite Hessian matrices.

To stabilize the optimization and isolate the most biologically parsimonious parameter space, we added ridge penalties to the negative log-likelihood. Covariate slopes (e.g., $\beta_{\text{SST}}$) were penalized toward a mean of 0 to shrink uninformative environmental effects and prevent overfitting. Similarly, baseline vital rate intercepts for survival and fecundity, which were estimated on the logit scale, were constrained using weakly informative normal penalties (mean = 0, SD = 1.5). On the natural probability scale, this gentle regularization restricts baseline rates to biologically plausible bounds (roughly 0.05 to 0.95). This prevents the optimization algorithms from pushing survival or fecundity to absolute 0 or 1—boundary values that can cause gradients to vanish and trigger numerical instability during matrix projections.

To ensure that our core ecological findings were not artifacts of these mathematical constraints, we conducted a rigorous sensitivity analysis. By systematically relaxing the penalty variances (e.g., widening the standard deviations for the fecundity and density dependence penalties) and profiling the likelihood surfaces, we verified that the model's emergent properties—specifically the carrying capacity ($K$) - was anchored by the empirical demographic data rather than the regularization structure itself.

*Estimating theoretical and realized carrying capacity:*

In highly variable marine ecosystems, traditional population models often confound climate-driven mortality with density-dependent limitation. Because previous models for this stock estimated carrying capacity by fitting a generalized logistic growth curve directly to reconstructed abundance time series, sudden population crashes driven by marine heatwaves could be mathematically interpreted as the population reaching its density-dependent ceiling. This approach likely underestimates the true biological potential of the stock. To resolve this, we utilized the mechanistic framework of the IPM, which simultaneously estimates the effects of population density and environmental variability (e.g., SST) on age-specific survival. By decoupling these factors, we defined and estimated two distinct carrying capacity metrics: theoretical *K* and realized *K*.

Because density dependence was parameterized mechanistically as a penalty on pup survival rather than through an overarching population growth curve, carrying capacity ($K$) was not estimated as an explicit parameter. Instead, $K$ was treated as an emergent property of the estimated vital rates. To propagate parameter uncertainty, we used the maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) and the model's precision matrix (Hessian) to generate 500 multivariate normal (MVN) parameter draws. For each draw, we developed a deterministic, sex-specific matrix projection model initialized with a small seed population and projected forward for 800 years to ensure the population achieved equilibrium and to mitigate the influence of short-term climate stochasticity. Survival and fecundity in the projection were dynamically updated at each time step based on the respective SST and density-dependence ($\beta_{DD}$) coefficients drawn for that iteration.

$$K=\lim_{t\to\infty}\sum_{a=1}^{25}N_{a,t}\quad\text{where}\quad N_{t+1}=N_{t}$$


Theoretical Carrying Capacity:
Theoretical *K* represents the absolute biological ceiling of the ecosystem based purely on space and baseline resources, absent of environmental extremes. To estimate Theoretical *K*, we projected the population forward holding the SST covariate constant at 0 (representing the mean-centered baseline temperature). Under this scenario, population growth is limited exclusively by the density-dependent penalty on pup survival. Theoretical *K* for each MVN draw was defined as the stabilized total abundance over the final years of the projection.

Realized Carrying Capacity:  
Because the California Current Ecosystem is characterized by frequent, cyclical marine heatwaves that acutely depress survival across multiple age classes, theoretical *K* is ecologically unrealistic. Therefore, we estimated realized *K*, defined as the long-term average abundance the population fluctuates around when subjected to historical frequencies of environmental variance. To estimate realized *K*, we subjected the simulated population to a dynamic thermal regime rather than a constant baseline. At each annual time step of the 800-year projection, an SST anomaly was drawn from a bootstrapped distribution of historical SST anomalies from 1990-2025. Realized *K* for each MVN draw was calculated as the mean total abundance over the final 400 years of the projection, ensuring the metric represented a stable dynamic equilibrium robust to decadal climate noise. 

*Estimation of MNPL and OSP Status*  

To evaluate the population status relative to the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) management metrics, we calculated the Maximum Net Productivity Level (MNPL) and Optimal Sustainable Population (OSP) status from the posterior draws of the $K$ simulations. MNPL was derived numerically by tracking the absolute population growth ($\Delta N$) at each time step of the *post-hoc* simulation. MNPL was identified as the population size where net production (the number of individuals added to the population annually) reached its global maximum:

$$MNPL=N_{t}\quad\text{where}\quad\max(N_{t+1}-N_{t})\text{ occurs}$$

To determine the stock's status relative to OSP, we compared the terminal year abundance estimate from the IPM ($N_{2024}$) to the calculated MNPL. A population is considered to be within its OSP if this ratio is greater than or equal to 1:

$$OSP_{status}=\frac{N_{current}}{MNPL}$$

This numeric derivation ensures that the management metrics are driven entirely by the species' empirical, age-structured vital rates and specific density-dependent survival thresholds estimated by the IPM.

##### Implementation and diagnostics 

The integrated population model was implemented in R (R Core Team 2024) using the RTMB package (citation), which leverages Template Model Builder (TMB) to evaluate the objective function via automatic differentiation (cite newest release). Annual fluctuations in fecundity were modeled as random effects and integrated out of the joint likelihood using the Laplace approximation. The negative log-likelihood was minimized using the nlminb optimization routine. Model convergence was confirmed by verifying that the maximum absolute gradient component of the objective function was near zero ($< 0.001$) and that the Hessian matrix was positive-definite, yielding standard errors for all fixed effects and derived parameters via the delta method. Structural identifiability of key parameter ridges (e.g., baseline fecundity and density dependence) was verified using likelihood profiling.

``` {r K plot sst, eval = T}
abline(h = real_K_CI[1], col = "darkred", lty = 3, lwd = 1.5)
abline(h = real_K_CI[2], col = "darkred", lty = 3, lwd = 1.5)

legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Mean trajectory", "95% CI", "Mean realized K", "95% CI"),
       col = c("blue", rgb(0, 0, 1, alpha = 0.15), "darkred", "darkred"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2, 3),
       lwd = c(2, 10, 2, 1.5),
       bty = "n")

```

#### Appendix

I still find myself skeptical of these tight and stable estimates, so I did my best to break the model in many ways. The biggest issue is that on paper, fecundity, SST effects, and density dependence are a bit confounded and fecundity is particularly not directly informed by data. I looked at the sensitivity of K to the standard deviations used in the ridge penalties and the flexibility I gave the model to adhere to pup counts. 


```{r k sensitivity, eval = T, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}

k_df <- read.csv(here('results', 'TMB', 'k_df_sensitivity.csv'), header = T, stringsAsFactors = F) %>%
  transform(Scenario = gsub('_', ' ', Scenario))

ggplot(k_df, aes(x = K_Estimate, y = Scenario, fill = Scenario)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, color = "gray30", trim = TRUE) +
  # median and 95% interquartile ranges
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", color = "black", outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(#title = "Sensitivity of carrying capacity (K) to model assumptions",
    # subtitle = "",
    x = "Estimated carrying capacity (total abundance)",
    y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = 'none') +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako", begin = 0.2, end = 0.8)

```

Figure A1. Sensitivity of carrying capacity (K) to ridge penalty scenarios. Distributions reflect 500 MVN parameter draws per scenario. Small differences here arise from differences in estimated density dependence and pup survival. 

```{r retro sens, eval = T, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 9}

retro_df <- read.csv(here('results', 'TMB', 'CSL_IPM_tmb_fec_sst_retro.csv'), header = T, stringsAsFactors = F)

plot_df <- retro_df %>%
  mutate(Lower = Estimate - (1.96 * Std_Error),
    Upper = Estimate + (1.96 * Std_Error),
    Data_Status = ifelse(is.na(Model_Input) & !is.na(Actual_Truth), 
                         "Forecast target", 
                         "Included in model")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Actual_Truth)) %>%   # Filter out years where there was no true survey conducted
  transform(sc = factor(Scenario, 
                        level = c('Drop_1_Years', 'Drop_2_Years', 'Drop_3_Years', 'Drop_4_Years', 'Drop_5_Years',
                                  'Drop_7_Years', 'Drop_10_Years'), 
                        labels = c('0', '1', '2', '3', '4', '6', '9')))

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = Year)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), fill = "dodgerblue", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Estimate), color = "dodgerblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Actual_Truth, fill = Data_Status, shape = Data_Status), 
             size = 1.5, color = "black") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("Included in model" = 21, "Forecast target" = 21)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Included in model" = "black", "Forecast target" = "red")) +
    facet_wrap(~sc, scales = "fixed") +
  # scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Retrospective sensitivity analysis",
    # subtitle = "Blue line indicates model expected pups; Red dots indicate withheld data",
    x = "", y = "Total pups",
    fill = "Data status", shape = "Data status") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", color = "black"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(1, 35, by = 5)), labels = c(seq(1991, 2025, by = 5)))

```

Figure A2. Sequentially removing more years (years shown in facets) of trailing pup count data (black/red) in a retrospective analysis shows strong ability to estimate (blue) removed pup counts up until 6+ years are removed, namely when SST was warm but pup counts stayed higher. I'm not sure what my thoughts are about this other than saying something about a non-stationary relationship between fecundity and SST, or that there was some other environmental factor that buffered negative SST effects on fecundity (but not survival) in 2016-2020 and 2023-2024.
